title: The system: SaaS invoicing and accounting on one PostgreSQL primary
caption: Every invoice, payment and ledger entry is committed on one primary and copied to a sync standby; reports, backups, search and analytics all hang off its WAL.

steps.text: A tenant's app issues an invoice or records a customer's payment through the Invoicing API. The API keeps no state, so it autoscales freely.
Thousands of API processes share a few hundred server connections: PgBouncer in transaction mode lends a connection for one transaction at a time.

On the primary, one transaction updates the invoice and writes balanced ledger entries (debit cash, credit receivables) into the current month's ledger partition. Constraints, not app code, refuse anything that doesn't add up.
The commit waits for the sync standby to flush the WAL, so a confirmed payment survives the loss of the primary's machine.
The same WAL streams asynchronously to read replicas, which serve aging reports and dashboards, and is archived with base backups for point-in-time recovery.
A logical replication slot feeds the CDC pipeline: only committed changes, in commit order, to the search index (find an invoice by number or customer) and the warehouse.

scenarios.name: Month-end close
scenarios.summary: The last two days of the month bring about 8× the usual writes plus the close jobs; the pooler, small batches and replicas keep the primary steady.

steps.text: Tenants issue their monthly invoices in bulk and the API scales out. PgBouncer queues the extra clients instead of opening thousands of backends on the primary.
Close jobs post accruals and revaluations in batches of a few hundred entries per transaction, so row locks and WAL bursts stay short and payments don't queue behind them.
Trial balances and aging reports run on the replicas. The final close report waits until the replica has replayed past the close's cut-off LSN, so it is complete yet off the primary.
The next month's ledger partition was created a week ago by a scheduled job, so the first payment posted on the 1st has somewhere to go.

scenarios.name: WAL archive stalls
scenarios.summary: Backups stop quietly, and WAL that can't be archived can't be recycled: the primary's disk fills unless someone notices.

steps.text: The archive bucket's credentials expire. archive_command starts failing for every WAL segment.
PostgreSQL keeps every segment that hasn't been archived. At month-end write rates pg_wal grows by gigabytes per hour on the primary's disk.

Replicas and the standby still work, so nothing looks wrong, but point-in-time recovery stopped at the last archived segment. Alerts on the archiver's failure count and pg_wal size are the only early signal.
Fix the credentials and the archiver catches up. Had the disk filled, the primary would have stopped accepting every write. A stalled CDC slot does the same, so cap it with max_slot_wal_keep_size.

scenarios.name: Retire a closed year
scenarios.summary: With monthly partitions, removing a year of ledger history is a metadata change, not a huge DELETE.

steps.text: Years older than the retention policy are no longer queried by the app; only an audit request ever needs them.
The job detaches each old month with DETACH PARTITION … CONCURRENTLY: payments keep posting into the current month untouched.
Each detached table is dumped to the archive bucket and dropped. No row-by-row delete, no dead tuples, no vacuum debt.
